item.title: Supermarkets Are the Next Big Challenge for Meat Reduction
item.description: We buy so much meat at grocery stores, so it's crucial to figure out how to lower animal product consumption in retail. I'm not convinced we've found a solution.
item.content:encoded:
Grocery stores are a crucial arena in the movement to change our food habits — in the US, a whopping three-fourths of calories are bought from supermarkets — so we need to think carefully about how to approach them. We have many options in front of us: offering more plant-based meat options, offering discounts, encouraging sales through banners or ads, or even reorganizing the aisles. The good news? This can boost alternative protein sales! The bad news? Meat sales don’t budge.

I think supermarkets are an unsolved problem. Let’s dive into the barriers we’re encountering and some potential ways to overcome them.

You’re reading More than Meat the Eye: a free newsletter on the science of meat reduction strategies. Check out my previous posts on nudge labeling and ratios for more behavioral science explanations!

Plant-Based Boosts Aren’t Enough

It´s difficult to talk about meat reduction in retail without discussing alternative proteins — they´re seen as the easiest way to shift shopping habits. Many supermarkets, especially those in Europe, have pledged to meaningfully boost sales of alternative proteins or reduce meat and animal product sales in the coming years. Lidl, for example, has committed to doubling sales of plant-based alternatives by 2030 and has already surpassed some of its initial targets! Various retailers in the Netherlands have taken a similar pledge, contributing to the decline of meat consumption in the country.

That´s about it for the good news, because there´s one big issue that kept popping up in my research: an increase in plant-based meat rarely occurred alongside a decrease in meat sales.

Most people who buy plant-based meat also buy animal-based meat, as high as 86%. Buying plant-based meat also isn’t associated with a later decrease in meat purchases. In other words, if someone picks up an Heura burger in a grocery store, that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s offsetting a meat purchase.

This trend persists when we examine interventions to promote plant-based meats. I charted several of these studies below. Keep in mind that most of these results aren’t statistically significant (meaning researchers aren’t sure whether the results are due to chance). This furthers my point: interventions to boost alternative proteins probably don’t reduce meat sales.

Reading this research was concerning — meaningfully reducing meat consumption in retail is far from being solved. We should also be extremely wary of supermarkets boasting about increased plant-based sales: if those numbers don’t come alongside a decrease in meat, not much is meaningfully being changed.

Why? I suspect one key factor is the consumer's flexibility. Many shoppers walk into grocery stores with a list of the needed items, either written down or implicitly memorized — something uncommon in restaurants. Also, grocery shoppers are often buying for others, such as a parent buying food for their entire family. It’s harder to shift someone into making a new decision for someone else, unlike a restaurant, where you’re just ordering for yourself.

There are benefits to increased plant-based options in grocery stores: they can make diet transitions easier for people and may help normalize plant-based eating. But I don’t see evidence that boosts to plant-based meat sales in retail are a win for meat reduction in and of themselves.

Subscribe now

We Need To Arrange Supermarkets Carefully

While reducing meat purchases is far from solved, there is plenty of research on boosting plant-based meat sales.

There has been much debate over whether meat alternatives should be placed in the meat section or in a vegetarian section. According to the research, the answer is… both! One real-world experiment found that having a “vegetarian shelf” and placing meat substitutes in the meat aisle led to a 32% sales boost, better than a veg shelf or meat aisle alone. Putting them in the meat aisle is still better than nothing: one study found that moving meat alternatives to the meat aisle led to a 25% boost in sales compared to the control, while a Lidl experiment showed this intervention boosted sales by 7%.

In other words, the ideal situation is to place meat alternatives throughout the store to encourage all types of consumers to purchase them, but having them just in the meat aisle is still better than segregating them in a veggie section, as most shoppers won´t wander that way at all. (By the way, studies show that consumers aren’t confused by terms like “plant-based meat”, despite what the EU has recently argued. So there is no marketing reason to avoid placing alternative proteins in the meat aisle, but Big Meat’s lobbying arm may make that difficult going forward.)

Some nudge studies also show promise. One online study found that nudges in an online supermarket could increase the percentage of plant-based items sold, but it had very high overall plant-based item availability: around 40%. To me, this suggests that nudges may be more effective if we can increase the ratio of plant-based products in supermarkets (see my earlier explainer for more details on ratios). Another study found that placing sustainable products more prominently and making them more available increased their uptake.

By far the largest sales boost I found was during a UK Veganuary promotion, which led to a 57% plant-based sales increase in January, declining to a smaller but respectable 15% boost in February onwards. This suggests that retail can benefit from aligning with broader cultural shifts, such as Veganuary, other vegan challenges, Meatless Mondays, or other large norm-setting events.

Other methods to reduce meat consumption haven’t found strong results. One experiment in an online supermarket found that adding various nudges (including tags like “increasingly chosen” and “check out these tasty products”) could only reduce meat purchases by 3%, an effect that wasn’t even statistically significant. Another thesis tested various nudges but didn’t find statistically significant results. One real-world study measured the impact of increasing the visibility of meat alternatives and whole foods plant-based options and adding signage throughout the store, even in shopping carts! There was a minor reduction in meat consumption, but again, it wasn’t statistically significant.

Taken together, supermarket nudges have a mixed track record.

Money is Key

The most critical way to influence shoppers is through price — a common theme in my resources! In one study, knocking a dollar off the price tag of meatless products increased their sales in an online grocery store and decreased meat selection (although it’s an online study, so it may not translate perfectly into the real world). Still, this finding matches broader research, like these two meta-analyses, which found that economic incentives worked better than educational or environmental interventions.

Crucially, price is the biggest factor in persuading frequent meat eaters to purchase plant-based products rather than animal-based ones. The same study estimated how much certain groups were willing to pay and found that frequent meat eaters needed far lower prices to consider buying plant-based products.

As I’ve explored before, plant-based diets are usually cheaper than animal-based ones, but alternative proteins are generally more expensive. In some countries, that’s changing. In Germany, plant-based alternatives are now cheaper than the meat they’re replacing. The cheaper they can get, the better.

The Bottom Line

Diving into this research, I hoped to find stronger results on the relationship between supermarket nudge interventions and meat reduction. Unfortunately, this isn’t a solved issue. To fix it, we’re going to research more novel ideas. It’s also going to require buy-in from the supermarkets themselves, which is why I’m hopeful that new organizations, like those that Charity Entrepreneurship are looking to build, can help drive these commitments.

In the meantime, we need to be using every tool in the toolbox simultaneously to achieve real results. Good labels probably won’t be enough. Prices won’t be enough. Rearranging aisles won’t be enough. When it comes to grocery stores, we need to go big or go home.

Thank you

item.title: Want People to Eat More Plants? Make Them the Default.
item.description: Making vegan foods the default option consistently boosts sales without significant backlash. Here's the evidence why it's so effective.
item.content:encoded:
In the developed world, meat is considered the default option. Waltz into most restaurants and it’s plain to see that main dishes feature oodles of animal products while plant-based foods are relegated to side dishes or even a separate menu. Airlines require passengers to opt into eating plant-based food onboard, usually ahead of time. Conferences, catering, delivery apps, dining halls… they all require consumers to put in just a little extra effort to eat meat-free. But we might be able to reverse that.

Plant-based defaults are a food service system in which vegan and vegetarian options are presented as the default. Customers can still eat meat! They just have to put in a little extra effort to do so: say, ordering ahead of time or talking to a staff member. This small change has a strong effect. The research shows that plant-based defaults (PBDs) are the most impactful nudge we know about — powerful enough to sway consumption trends but not controversial enough to inspire significant resistance. Let’s dive into it.

This is my final post on the effectiveness of plant-based nudges — check out my earlier editions on vegan labelling, plant-to-animal ratios, and supermarket design. If you want to stay up-to-date on the research behind effective animal advocacy, you can subscribe to this newsletter.

Making Plants the Default Option Works Wonders

What does a plant-based default look like in practice? It depends on the location. At conferences or events, guests may be automatically offered the veg option unless they fill out a form to switch to an animal-based meal. In cafeterias, buffets, and dining halls, customers may need to ask staff to fetch meat dishes from the back while plant-based options are front and center. In restaurants, defaults are a bit tricky but still doable. The dishes may be plant-based by default, with customers able to add animal products for an extra charge. Think a burrito with soya meat, which you can swap for chicken for an extra three bucks.

Here´s what a plant-based default looks like in a college dining hall (taken from this study):

Note how the meat dish is still available in the plant-based default (photo B), but students will have to ask the staff to fetch it from the back. This small extra effort will deter many students from ordering the less sustainable meal.

And boy, oh boy, does this work. Across the board, defaults are the most consistent way to influence plant-based eating in dining institutions. Full stop. Not only have several studies found them to be the best nudge available, but my own research shows their power quite clearly:

To review all the studies in detail, click here.

Across all the studies I could find, when meat is presented as the default option, consumers order vegan meals around 19% of the time. When plant-based options are the default, that number skyrockets to 69%. That’s an increase of a factor of 3.7. To put it bluntly: most interventions to reduce meat consumption are not this consistent, nor this powerful.

Many other meat reduction interventions aim to persuade people to make more ethical, sustainable, healthful, or conscious choices when dining out, but they don’t always work because people don´t always make decisions consciously. The beauty of a plant-based default lies in its simplicity — since most consumers go with the flow when ordering food, let’s change the tide rather than make them swim upstream.

Working With Institutions To Implement PBDs

There are many benefits to a plant-based default that aren’t just related to meat consumption. For starters, plant-based food is usually the most inclusive option — it allows vegetarians, vegans, people who follow kosher or halal diets, Jains, Hindus, Buddhists, lactose-intolerant individuals (which is most people by the way), and people with egg allergies to eat freely.

It can also save money! As I’ve written about previously, vegan diets are typically cheaper than animal-based diets, so it stands to reason that plant-based defaults can save on procurement costs. One study of New York City hospitals found that the plant-based default meals saved 59 cents per plate. And, of course, because plant-based food is more sustainable, plant-based defaults can reduce climate emissions, up to 42%.

One of the beautiful things about PBDS is that, with multiple benefits, there are many ways to approach stakeholders: public events with diverse audiences may want to be more inclusive with food options, while colleges with climate commitments can show how they’re reducing emissions.

These policies are more popular than you might think. Since plant-based defaults don’t remove choice, most consumers are more open to PBDs than an entirely plant-based menu. It makes sense! Anyone who truly craves meat would order the meat option rather than complain to the staff. When researchers survey diners in a plant-based default, they don’t find that anyone is angry or upset about the change.

One study found that consumers are more accepting of plant-based defaults than restaurant managers are, suggesting that managers are too concerned about public blowback. Thankfully, that blowback is rare: most PBDs have satisfaction rates above 90%. These policies are popular; it’s just about getting institutions like colleges, hospitals, public events, and more to buy into them.

Long-Term Impacts of Plant-Based Defaults

College dining halls are where defaults may work best, since they may offer benefits beyond just short-term meat reduction. Campuses are hubs for young adults learning about social norms and practices, so if we can make plant-based eating extremely normalized for huge cohorts of young people, it can have ripple effects for generations. I couldn’t find research proving that PBDs can influence social norms, but I suspect they can. I’d love to see more researchers study this.

There is a problem with diner retention — some studies have found that potential consumers may not attend the dining halls when a plant-based default is instituted, and instead eat meat at another establishment (researchers call it the ‘spillover effect’). Two studies reported pessimistic data: one found that instituting a plant-based default correlated with a 26% reduction of overall sales, while another found that instituting a meat-free day was associated with a 17% sales decrease.

Since very few studies actually check for spillover, I looked at the data tables from other studies and did some back-of-the-napkin math to discover how big a problem spillover really is. In one study, college students ordered 20% more meals when a plant-based default was implemented, compared to a standard meat default. To me, it remains an open question whether an adverse spillover effect exists and, if so, how big a problem it is.

Even if a spillover effect exists consistently, it is likely smaller than the intervention´s benefits. In other words, fewer people skip eating at the PBD station than people who switch from meat to vegan, so the number of people eating plant-based food still rises.

Tracking the Spread of Plant-Based Defaults

Overall, PBDs are highly effective in reducing meat consumption and are less likely to incur blowback or criticism than many other interventions. As long as they’re implemented well, we can minimize potential spillover effects and maybe even shift social norms around how we eat.

I’ve been researching interventions to reduce meat consumption for years now. I can say confidently that plant-based defaults are the initiative that excites me most. It’s that perfect combination of palatable, scalable, and impactful work that can really move the needle.

I’m hoping my series on behavioral science has helped you think more about these interventions! But that’s not the only reason I wrote this — I am working on formally tracking these interventions to show how effective they are, give credit to the organizations that work on them, and demonstrate how this social movement is progressing. item.title: The Consequences of Factory Farming Are Too Large to Ignore
item.description: Factory farming is often brushed aside as a niche concern, but it's one of the largest—and most ignored—sources of suffering, environmental destruction, and human harm in the world today.
item.content:encoded:
As this newsletter has grown, I’ve started to reach new audiences, ones who don’t already buy into the importance of meat reduction. That’s great! I love reaching new people! But, to make sure we are all on the same page, I’ve decided to write out the definitive reasons why I think meat reduction is a critical social issue, likely the most overlooked social issue in our society today.

Entire books can be written about this topic (in fact, many have), but I aim to summarize the most important facts and arguments here, organized into harms to animals, the environment, and humans. Consider this resource comprehensive but not exhaustive: a way to distill the reasons behind meat reduction advocacy and clarify our mission going forward.

Animal Agriculture is a Moral Atrocity — Here’s Why

If you’re reading this, chances are that you’re an animal lover. I am too! I believe animals are individuals, worthy of consideration and care, and deserving of a life of beauty and free from suffering. Unfortunately, our species has designed a food production system that doesn’t live up to those ideals.

Most people’s mental images of animal farms — red barns, green fields, and overall-wearing ranchers — don’t match reality. In agriculture, factory farming is the norm, not an exception. In the United States, over 99% of animals raised for food are raised on factory farms, while worldwide it’s 94%. Factory farms are characterized by confining many animals in super tiny spaces, often in cages, and depriving them of sunlight, access to the outdoors, or even the ability to be with their friends and family.

This confinement creates huge problems for animals. Most farmers define welfare as animals being free from disease or injury, which isn’t exactly how most people think of welfare. If you had a healthy dog who lived her entire life in a kennel without access to sunlight, toys, nature, or other animals, would you define that as high welfare? I personally wouldn’t. Even farms with higher welfare standards suffer from this problem: the mental states of farmed animals are completely ignored. Research backs up what you and I see: hens in cages exhibit symptoms of depression.

The types of animals on farms matter too. Have you ever met one of those dogs, like a bulldog or pug, that has been selectively bred for so long that their genetics now cause serious breathing problems? Well, the exact same thing is happening to farmed animals, except they’re being genetically bred to grow faster and fatter, not to maximize cuteness. Chickens, turkeys, cows, pigs, and more have all been getting fatter and fatter, which is great for producing cheap meat but an absolute disaster for welfare. Chickens can now develop heart disease in their first few months of life; pigs grow fatter and produce more piglets per litter; hens lay far more eggs than before.

The scale of the problem today exceeds human comprehension. Every year, we slaughter 85 billion land animals, 300 billion aquatic animals, and 100 billion insects. For contrast, about 62 million humans die every year — a rounding error compared to farmed animals. My graphing software is literally incapable of showing a percentage that small visually:

Most people probably believe that humans are more morally valuable than animals. Even if that’s true, if you believe that animal lives are worth 100 times less than human lives (heck, even 10,000 times less!), the sheer scale of animals trapped in factory farms would mean that farmed animal suffering has moral worth.

If you’ve ever spent significant time with an animal, you probably already know what researchers have confirmed: they can feel pain, they have inner lives, they experience a spectrum of emotions, can use tools, create their own cultures, and they bond fiercely with one another. Yes, even fish. Animals aren’t cogs in a machine that we can wipe away from our moral framework. They matter.

Animal Agriculture is Gobbling Up Land and Choking the Planet

There are two main ways that animal agriculture harms the planet: directly (through greenhouse gas emissions) and indirectly (through land use change, especially deforestation).

Ruminant animals like cows and sheep naturally emit methane as a part of their digestive system processing — you might have heard that they have multiple stomachs. Well, all those stomachs produce a lot of gas. When we combine those emissions with other things like manure, we are looking at 16.5% of global emissions, at a minimum1. That seems like a lot! But we have to remember that the number of animals bred into existence now is not natural — it’s human-designed. 57% of mammals on Earth by biomass are farmed, while wild animals are only 5%. There’s nothing natural about how we farm animals.

However, in my opinion, land-use change is more important than direct emissions and is far less discussed. About 35% of Earth’s land is used for animal agriculture. Why? It’s not just the animal farms and slaughterhouses, but also for all the plots of corn, soy, and wheat that are grown to make animal feed. If you’ve ever gone on a road trip through rural areas and seen rows and rows of corn stalks, those farms are probably growing food for animals, not humans.

Animal agriculture’s land use footprint is driving deforestation across the world. 41% of global tropical deforestation is driven by beef production. All of this land could be rewilded, which has the potential to offset 68% of all human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

“When you eat a burger, you’re not just eating a cow. You’re eating macaws and jaguars and the rest of the cast of Rio. You’re eating the Amazon. You’re eating the earth.” – Michael Grunwald

All of this land use change harms biodiversity by robbing native species of their homes. (Keep in mind that “biodiversity loss” is scientist-speak for animals or plants going extinct or endangered). Animal products, alongside specific plant-based crops like coffee, are supercharging extinction rates worldwide. A recent study quantified how this looks compared to several diets:

Taken together, vegan diets have one-fourth the carbon footprint of high-meat diets, one-third the negative impact on biodiversity, and half of the impact on water usage.

I want to stress that this research is rock-solid, decades-old, and not meaningfully debated in the scientific community. Scholars from FAO, Nature, World Resources Institute, Science, The Lancet, Frontiers, Greenpeace, Cambridge, Oxford, and many more all agree — animal farming is a massive threat to Earth and her inhabitants. Anything to the contrary is likely part of Big Meat’s disinformation campaign, which they borrowed from Big Oil.

Humans Are Victims As Much As Animals

The lives of humans and animals are deeply intertwined, so much so that it’s impossible to talk about harms to one without discussing harms to the other. This is the bedrock for a concept called “One Health”: an approach to optimize the health of people, animals, and environments alike.

Factory farms and slaughterhouses are hotbeds for labor rights abuses: frequently hiring vulnerable populations like undocumented immigrants, who comprise 37-47% of U.S. farm laborers, since the job is so unpleasant. Children, too. Meat companies like JBS and Tyson are embroiled in child labor lawsuits left and right. Meat workers routinely make up some of the most dangerous professions possible, according to data from OSHA — 81% of meatpackers are at risk of serious injury, while agriculture has the highest worker death rate of any industry worldwide.

“[…] The United States is failing to meet its obligations under international human rights standards to protect the human rights of meat and poultry industry workers.” — Human Rights Watch

Slaughterhouse workers are usually people who don’t have any other options: in order to feed their families, they are forced to commit acts of violence on animals, which takes a massive toll. They often suffer from a condition known as perpetration-induced traumatic stress, in which they experience emotional detachment and increased aggression as a result of enacting violence on animals. This can’t be reformed — a higher minimum wage or better labour unions can help with some things, but they can’t undo the psychic pressure from constant killing. Only reducing meat demand can do that.

There’s a better way. Investing in plant-based agriculture, especially alternative protein, could also create jobs and boost the economy. As I explored in an earlier piece, a shift to a vegan diet can create 83 million new jobs by 2050 and potentially save 7 trillion USD.

It’s not just workers who’d benefit from meat reduction, but everyone who eats meat themselves. Since animal protein is a significant risk factor in developing many chronic diseases like heart disease, some types of cancer, diabetes, and all-cause mortality, a FAO report estimates that dietary shifts to veganism could save 14 million lives.

Animal agriculture even harms vegans, albeit indirectly. Animal agriculture has caused 37% of zoonotic diseases in the last 80 years. Factory farms also account for 70% of all antibiotics worldwide, increasing the threat of antibiotic-resistant superbugs. Taken together, it’s no surprise that the UN listed “increasing demand for animal protein” as the number one driver of emerging zoonotic diseases like COVID-19. I don’t want to repeat 2020, do you?

This Problem is Expected to Worsen

Unfortunately, consumption of animal products is expected to rise over the next few decades. For starters, the human population is expected to grow, but more importantly, people tend to eat more meat as their incomes rise — in fact, average income is the best predictor of a country’s level of meat consumption.

This means that meat reduction will become more and more important as time ticks on. A recent paper found that 44% of the Earth’s population needs to change their diets (primarily through meat reduction) to achieve only 2 degrees of global warming (keep in mind, if you are a citizen of a developed country who eats meat, you are almost certainly in that 44% bucket). By 2050, it will be 91% of people. In other words, big meat-eaters are fueling climate change now and will make it even worse in the future.

Unlike poverty, infant mortality, literacy, child labor, or life expectancy, meat consumption is expected to get worse before it gets better. Unlike climate change, we haven’t seen meaningful meat reduction policies or global summits a la the Paris Climate Accords. This problem is horribly neglected.

I’m a data guy. I love seeing rows and rows of beautiful columns, charts, and graphs, each one giving me more insight about how the world around me works. But sometimes I have to stop myself and remember that every single number represented here is an individual, deserving of the same care and respect we would give a pet. A tiny uptick on this chart represents billions of animals, animals who can feel pain, experience joy, and express community. It also represents tons more greenhouse gases clogging the atmosphere and millions of people who experience worse health as a result. We need to figure out how to make the line go down.

Every Potential Solution Involves Meat Reduction. Every Single One.

Usually, this is where the conversation stops: yes, factory farming is bad for animals, humans, and the planet, so we should reform it. But there’s another fact, usually omitted from the conversation, that some people may find uncomfortable: there is no way to fix our food system without changing our collective diets, specifically reducing meat consumption. None. Zilch. Zero.

Don’t get me wrong: some systems improve upon our existing reality, but for any of them to work, they need to involve changes to our diets. Take regenerative agriculture. It’s a loosely defined set of farming practices designed to improve soil health, including holistic grazing, in which ruminant animals graze across different pastures to enhance soil health. Advocates claim regenerative agriculture can be carbon-negative because the benefits to the soil’s carbon sequestration outweigh the cows’ methane emissions.

Even if this were true, there’s one massive problem: land. According to an industry-funded study, a fully regenerative system can sequester carbon… but would require 2.5 times the land we currently use2. Okay, let’s do the math here: animal agriculture currently uses 4 billion hectares of land, so if we switched conventional agriculture to regenerative, we’d need 10 billion hectares, which is about half of all land on Earth!

Switching from beef to chicken may be a small win for the climate, but a disaster for animal welfare. Since chickens are so small, we need to kill 200 times as many individuals to produce the same amount of meat as a single cow (researchers call this the small body problem). Meat reduction is really the only way to benefit both the climate and the animals.

I’ve researched other potential climate solutions before, and none of them hold up. Red seaweed used to be a hot topic until recent real-world studies failed to find any meaningful improvement. Grass-fed and local meat completely fall flat. Methane masks? Give me a break.

The data is clear: there is no way to eat meat that’s more sustainable than eating less of it.

Or let’s consider animal welfare. Farmers aren’t cruel to their animals because they’re psychopaths, but because it’s the most efficient way to meet growing demand for meat. To produce 360 million tonnes of meat worldwide annually, animal farmers choose fast-growing breeds, cram animals together to maximize space, and breed them as quickly as possible to increase production. If they increased welfare, they would not be able to meet current demand.

Researchers agree — there is no way to make our food production more sustainable and ethical without significantly reducing our meat consumption. Maybe there is a future in which most people eat animals raised on green pastures, who grew up munching on organic foods while playing together in the sunlight. But that is only possible if everyone eats meat once, maybe twice a week.

Subscribe now

When I started this Substack, I debated framing it around factory farming, but I ultimately decided it wasn’t good enough. There’s an elephant in the room we need to address: there is no meaningful anti-factory farming position without meat reduction.

Opposing Factory Farming is a Maintream Opinion

There’s one powerful fact at our disposal: most people already oppose factory farming, at least in principle. When polled, a large majority of people say that animals deserve moral consideration, that they’re concerned about factory farming practices, or even that we should restrict or abolish factory farming altogether.

While people have an innate sense that factory farming is wrong, they typically support it economically. This represents a departure from other historical social movements: meat reduction is popular, but difficult to achieve. Other movements — marriage equality, civil rights, women’s suffrage — faced the opposite problem: minimal public support but less impact on others’ lives. It’s a double-edged sword. On the one hand, changes in people’s lives may create barriers, but the underlying level of agreement can help forge coalitions to drive change.

Meat Reduction Is a Nascent, But Fervent, Social Movement

There are countless organizations working to reduce meat consumption. Alternative protein companies number in the thousands — from Heura to Impossible Foods to Essential to Omni — and are scaling up more sustainable and ethical foods worldwide, while incubators like the Good Food Institute work to secure more funding and legal rights.

Many groups are working to get people accustomed to meat reduction, little by little. Veganuary has successfully helped 25 million people go vegan for one month each year, of whom 81%3 maintain a reduced meat diet afterwards. Better Food Foundation (a group I frequently work with) is helping redesign social norms around meat by making plants the default option. Other groups, like Proveg or Dansk Vegetarisk Forening, are lobbying governments to create more laws to promote plant-based foods, such as investing in alternative proteins, removing animal ag subsidies, and regulating meat companies more closely. There are countless more, on every continent4, with dozens of strategies, ideas, and missions.

Still, I believe this issue is extremely neglected. When’s the last time you heard someone on the news talk about meat reduction in a sincere way? Do you have any politicians representing you who have voted for resolutions to work on meat consumption? How often do you hear climate advocates talking about agriculture or meat consumption as a campaign goal? One reason is that meat reduction isn’t very well funded. Global funding for animal protection NGOs is only about $250 million, which sounds like a lot until you realize that it’s about the same as the salaries of a single Premier League football team. There is a lot of room for growth here — imagine what we could do with double, triple, quintuple that amount.

It’s an uphill battle, but we’re making some headway. Meat consumption in the EU is expected to fall 1.3% over the next decade, driven by huge reductions in plant-forward countries like Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden.

It’s not enough, not nearly enough, but it is promising.

You’ve Come to the Right Place

Well, that’s my pitch! I believe reducing our collective consumption of meat is not only imperative for the future of humanity, animal-kind, and the Earth, but it is also one of the most neglected social issues of our time. The planet matters. Humans, embroiled in factory farming operations or not, matter. And, of course, animals matter.

If you understand why reducing meat is important, this Substack is for you. I don’t care if you’re vegan, vegetarian, flexitarian, or a meat-lover — it’s your motivation that matters, not your diet. Here, I am less interested in the why and more in the how. How do we scale up meat reduction initiatives? What are the best policies to pursue? What psychological and sociological factors do we need to consider?

Change is never easy, but it is always possible. Let’s chip away at it together.

In other words, transitioning from animal-based to plant-based food systems is still always better than transitioning from conventional to regenerative agricultural practices.

item.title: Banks Are Bankrolling Factory Farms 32x More Than Alternative Proteins
item.description: How banks are quietly funnelling hundreds of billions into industrial animal agriculture — and what we can do about it.
item.content:encoded:
Most social ills don’t emerge from nowhere: they’re heavily funded systems borne out of corporate interests and buoyed by heaps of cash. Factory farming is no different.

In the past few decades, "fossil fuel financing" has become a popular talking point among climate activists — if we can get banks to divest from oil and gas companies and invest in renewable energy, we can slow climate change. The logic also applies to our food systems. Enter: “factory farm financing“, a critical economic lever for change. If we want to reduce meat consumption at a meaningful scale, we need to level the playing field by pressuring banks to stop funding industrial animal agriculture and instead pour that money into more ethical, sustainable alternatives. Here’s how we can start.

The Scale of Factory Farm Financing

When you deposit money into your bank account, it doesn’t just sit there — banks use up to 90% of that cash to generate more money. Some of it is lent out to regular people (think small-business loans or mortgages) at higher interest rates so banks can make a profit. But another chunk of that cash is invested in bonds and stocks, including for corporations that aren’t so ethical. That means that when you hold your money in a bank account, your money may be loaned out to factory farm giants — like JBS, Tyson, or Minerva — without you even knowing about it.

How much? It’s difficult to say for certain, since many of these investments aren’t widely publicized. Still, a recent Foodrise report found that the 55 largest livestock companies received over 600 billion US dollars from 2015 to 2022:

This money has allowed factory farming giants like Tyson and JBS to consolidate their market power, especially by gobbling up smaller companies and streamlining their operations. Over time, it also legitimizes factory farming as an institution — social influence as well as economic.

But the issue of factory farm finance and greenwashing doesn’t stop with retail banks. The UN’s Green Climate Fund invested 175 million into animal agriculture, and the World Bank invested almost $2 billion into industrial meat, dairy, and feed operations. The majority of this money, 77%, is going to industrial animal agriculture (a term more or less synonymous with ‘factory farming’).

Given that we produce about 350 billion kilograms of meat every year, bank investments in factory farming amount to about 25 cents per kilogram. However, this money is primarily being used not to keep meat prices low, but to spread factory farming in places where it hasn’t yet taken root, especially in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America. This means that reducing factory farming financing is especially important in mitigating the spread of animal agriculture, even if it won’t raise meat prices in rich countries very much.

As I have written before, the development of factory farming in Africa is extremely concerning — while improving food production is important for global health, the rapid investment in factory farms by wealthy foreign investors will cause significant harm to animals and African communities. Better solutions include scaling up the production of alternative proteins and intensifying plant-based agriculture. However, that’s not where the money is going — banks’ investments in factory farming alone are 32 times those in alternative proteins.

Animal ethics matter too: banks could choose to finance farms with higher welfare standards, but most don’t. According to Sinergia Animal’s bank ranking, 78% of the banks they reviewed have zero ethical requirements for investing in factory farms.

On nearly all metrics — ethics and sustainability alike — banks are failing to lead the way, and consumers don’t have any idea. We need to change that.

Lessons from the Fossil Fuel Movement

The fossil fuel divestment movement has been campaigning for well over a decade now to stop pumping money into Big Oil; however, the evidence on its impact is mixed. On the one hand, the number of large banks with some form of climate investment policy has nearly doubled since 2015. On the other, there has been no decline in fossil fuel lending since the Paris Agreement:

However, several studies have shown large differences in fossil fuel spending by country — places like Europe are doing well while others, like Canada and Japan, aren’t. Countries with more divestment commitments also have less FFF financing, particularly driven by NGO commitments. This correlation indicates that while the FFF movement hasn’t stopped the flow of money, it has been able to mitigate it.

Public institutions are also outperforming private ones; for example, the 40 public signatories to the Clean Energy Transition Partnership have reduced fossil fuel financing by 78% over the past few years. Taken together, it’s clear that fighting unsustainable financing is an uphill battle, but activists are slowly chipping away at it.

To scale down factory farming and accelerate the food transition, we need to do the same. Luckily for us, the playbook from the energy transition and a swathe of research are already at our fingertips.

What We Can Do About It

First up: spread awareness of the problem, motivating people to switch from banks that invest in factory farming or otherwise signal their dissatisfaction to their banks. The good news is that most people don’t support factory farming — up to 90% of people would support transitioning from factory farms to a more humane, sustainable form of agriculture. We need to tap into this sentiment.

I suspect that people are far more likely to support a shift away from factory farming financing than they are to change their diets. Take, for example, something called the “vote-buy gap” — a phenomenon in which people are more likely to vote for legislation that impacts animals (say, banning the use of cages in farms) than take action that the same legislation would create (i.e., buying cage-free eggs). The same may be true for banking. If one’s choice of banks is the same as voting with their wallets, they may be more likely to pressure or switch banks than they are to boycott factory-farmed meat. This opens up entire legions of potential allies, broadening the coalition.

Lobbying for public divestment also has many indirect benefits: it can signal a larger social shift, which could deter future investments and general positive media coverage. Take the story of Jordi Casamitjana, a British citizen who was fired from his job after objecting to his employer for investing his pension fund into companies that harm the environment and test products on animals. He subsequently sued his employer and won, showing that employees often have the power to direct their funds.

These narratives and lobbying efforts can, over time, create a powerful stigma against investing in factory farming. A 2022 report from Animal Ask argues that the potential stigmatizing effects of a divestment campaign are likely its most important components. This stigma has two benefits: it reduces the likelihood that banks will invest in factory farming and further normalizes and legitimizes the movement to stop it, thereby creating a larger pro-animal, pro-environment coalition.

We also need to talk about money (something I’ve argued we don’t do enough of). The climate movement showed that divesting from fossil fuels wouldn’t harm the returns for big banks, meaning that banks that invested with their conscience wouldn’t lose any money. We can create the same narrative for factory farming and even show that investing in Big Meat is economically risky. One report found that 28 issues related to factory farming investments could harm returns, including increased pandemic risk and environmental litigation. Another report found that up to 235 billion pounds of EU and UK investments may be at risk if diets continue to change. If we can demonstrate that investing in Big Meat is risky for banks, they’ll be less likely to do so.

To play devil’s advocate: how likely is it that a single bank´s refusal to finance a factory farm company would affect other investments — in other words, is it possible that another bank would swoop in and fund the project, resulting in the same number of animals being farmed? Let’s examine research on fossil fuel financing. A 2022 study found that coal firms subjected to strict bank divestment policies cut their borrowing by 25% compared to peers — and that this translated into real emissions reductions, particularly because the coal industry relies on capital from a small number of banks, leaving companies with few alternative financing options. However, the authors note that private sector action alone is insufficient.

That’s where norms and regulations come into play: by creating industry standards, we can ensure that no single bank can swoop in and fund new factory farms. Some researchers argue that regulation could create a tipping point and ensure long-term change. They could even create a positive feedback loop, where green investments increase policies which increase green investments — a virtuous cycle. That’s why we will need comprehensive frameworks to evaluate how rapidly banks are phasing out factory farming investing, which will allow us to compare sectors easily.

Individual actions are only part of the solution, but a necessary precursor to systemic change.

The Bottom Line

Shifting Big Banks’ money away from factory farming won’t be easy, but a sustained effort from individuals and organizations may eventually chip away at the problem. If we can create a feedback loop in which consumer actions, industry regulations, and investment norms work together to promote more ethical and sustainable investing, we can help mitigate the expansion of factory farming.
